A rush of diggers to the diamond fields of the dry interior of southern Africa after rich finds in 1871 on a farm owned by the De Beer brothers. The mining camp, first called New Rush, became the town of Kimberley.

Thousands of claims were dug side by side, by hand, into what became the Big Hole. Britain annexed the area as Griqualand West in 1871, over the claims of the Orange Free State and local Griqua and Tswana leaders.

Kimberley set patterns that shaped modern South Africa:

  • Tens of thousands of African men came as migrant workers, often to earn guns, and were housed in closed compounds.
  • Small claims were merged into big companies. Cecil Rhodes won out over Barney Barnato and formed De Beers in 1888.
  • Diamond fortunes and mining skills paid for the Witwatersrand gold rush after 1886.

It turned the region from farming to mining and drew Britain deeper into the interior.
